title: The Stolen Purse

full_text:
An affluent merchant from Basra arrived at a crowded public bathhouse in Cairo, carrying a velvet purse containing five hundred gold dinars, heavily perfumed with rare, genuine ambergris which he had purchased in the spice market.

After completing his bath, he went to his dressing alcove, only to find that his velvet purse had been stolen. He raised an outcry, but thirty citizens were present in the hall, and each protested his innocence.

The merchant summoned the famous magistrate of Cairo, Abu Bakr.

The magistrate did not threaten the bathers with torture or chains. He ordered the outer portals locked, gathered all thirty bathers in the central steam hall, and commanded: 'Let every man step forward and wash his hands in this basin of boiling rosewater, and then dry them upon this clean white linen towel!'

One by one, the bathers washed their hands and dried them.

The magistrate smelled the towel after each bather. When the twenty-third man dried his hands, the magistrate caught the unmistakable, rich fragrance of ambergris clinging to the linen! The thief, in seizing the purse, had absorbed the persistent aromatic oil into the pores of his fingers, which even hot water could not erase.

The magistrate looked sternly at the man: 'Produce the velvet purse from your boot!'

The trembling thief, astonished that his own scent had betrayed him, pulled the purse from his boot and confessed his crime.

The magistrate restored the gold to the merchant and punished the thief, demonstrating that justice investigates the subtle evidence of nature rather than relying upon noisy accusations.
moral: The subtle traces of truth cannot be washed away; keen observation unmasks the most elusive thief.
